They run 2, and the split is never about the model.
The second agent is not redundancy but a different seat, and the two rarely get separated.
Which seat owns your repo right now? If both do, you ship the conflict to production. Here is the exact 2-seat runbook, and why the real cost is not tokens but the merge nobody reviewed.
One agent lives inside the IDE. It stays close to the file, the cursor, the type errors, and the thought currently in motion.
Another lives in the terminal. It gets a bounded mission, works across the repository, runs commands, checks its own work, and returns with evidence.
This is first-hand operator framing, not a market survey with invented percentages. The as-of 2026 pattern I see across public builder workflows, tool releases, and my own use is simple: capable operators are separating interactive flow from delegated execution.
The distinction matters more than which two logos they choose.
Buy two seats without defining the jobs, and you get duplicate context, conflicting edits, extra review, and a larger bill. Split the work correctly and the second agent can pay rent by removing whole missions from your active attention.
The operating model I use is:
IDE agent for flow. Terminal agent for missions.
The rest of this article explains where that split works, where it fails, and how to install it without turning your repository into an agent playground.
At the end, you will get the copy-paste Two-Agent Seat Map I use to decide ownership, control handoffs, and audit whether the second seat still earns its cost.
One agent becomes two bad jobs stapled together
 
A single coding agent looks tidy on a tooling diagram.
You open one product, give it repository access, and ask it to help with everything. It completes lines, explains code, searches files, runs tests, writes migrations, reviews diffs, and sometimes takes a large task from prompt to pull request.
The problem appears during real work.
Interactive coding and delegated coding have different operating needs.
When I am shaping an API, repairing a component, or tracing a type through three files, I want short feedback loops. I want to point at a symbol, reject a suggestion, change direction, and keep the unfinished model in my head. The agent should remain near my cursor and respond to small changes in intent.
A repository mission has the opposite shape.
“Find why the background worker duplicates deliveries, patch the cause, add regression coverage, and report the commands you ran” should not require constant cursor steering. It needs room to search, form a hypothesis, edit several files, execute tests, inspect failures, and return a compact account.
Force both jobs through one conversation and the context starts to rot.
The agent remembers an early instruction after the task has changed. A broad implementation request sits beside half a dozen tiny edits. Test output consumes the same thread used for design reasoning. You hesitate to start another task because the current session contains details you may need later.
Then human behavior makes it worse. You keep checking the agent because it occupies the same surface where you are trying to work. Delegation becomes supervised typing.
I have also seen the reverse failure. A builder uses a terminal agent for every tiny change. They launch a mission to rename a prop, wait for repository inspection, review a broad diff, and spend more attention than the edit deserved.
One seat is not automatically cheaper if it taxes every task with the wrong interaction model.
The two-agent setup begins with a job split, not a vendor split. If both agents can claim any task, you have installed ambiguity. If each seat has a clear unit of work, you have built a small operating system.
The IDE seat protects the live reasoning loop
 
The IDE agent belongs inside the work I am actively thinking through.
I use it when the next decision depends on what I will learn from the next small edit. The task may be difficult, but it is locally interactive.
Good IDE seat work includes:
Completing a function whose contract I already understand
Explaining an unfamiliar symbol while I inspect its callers
Drafting a test beside the implementation
Repairing a type error exposed by my current change
Refactoring a selected block while preserving behavior
Producing two local alternatives I can compare immediately
Following an error from the editor into one or two related files
The IDE seat gets rich local context without ceremony. It sees the open file, selection, nearby diagnostics, and often the language server. That makes it useful for precise intervention.
Its main output is momentum.
I do not measure this seat by how much code it writes. I measure whether it shortens the distance between an idea and the next informed decision. Sometimes the best response is five lines. Sometimes it is an explanation that stops me from editing the wrong abstraction.
The control loop stays human-led:
I choose the next local objective.
The agent proposes or explains.
I inspect the result in place.
The compiler, type checker, or focused test responds.
I decide the next move.
This seat should be interruptible. I expect to redirect it without producing a formal handoff every time. The unfinished reasoning remains mine.
That freedom creates a boundary.
I do not give the IDE seat a vague repository-wide task while I continue editing related files. I have tried versions of that workflow. The agent searches with partial context, edits files outside my current view, and collides with changes I made during its run. Review becomes archaeology.
A useful test is whether I can define the task by pointing.
“Change this parser to accept the new field” belongs in the IDE.
“Find every producer and consumer affected by the field, update them, run the relevant suite, and identify migration risk” is a mission. It belongs elsewhere.
The IDE agent is strongest when the work benefits from proximity. Treating it as a background employee wastes that advantage.
The terminal seat owns missions with a finish line
The terminal agent gets work that can be bounded by outcome, scope, and verification.
I use it for repository searches, multi-file changes, test repair, dependency investigations, migration preparation, documentation updates tied to code, and review passes with explicit criteria.
A good mission prompt contains five things:
The observed problem
The desired end state
The permitted scope
The checks required before completion
The expected return format
For example:
Diagnose why webhook retries can create duplicate ledger entries. Work inside the webhook, ledger, and related test modules. Preserve the public API. Add regression coverage for the confirmed cause. Run the narrow tests first, then the relevant suite. Return the cause, changed files, commands, results, and remaining risk.
That prompt gives the agent a mission rather than a mood.
The terminal surface helps because the repository becomes the working environment. Search results, diffs, test processes, build output, and version control state are available in one operational loop. The agent can inspect before editing and verify after editing.
Its main output is a completed change with evidence.
The terminal seat should not return “done” as a status. It should return receipts:
Root cause or implementation rationale
Files changed
Tests added or updated
Commands executed
Results observed
Checks not run
Assumptions and remaining risk
This is where the second seat can remove real cognitive load. I can keep designing another part of the system while the mission proceeds, provided the file ownership does not overlap.
That last clause carries the whole setup.
Parallel agents do not create safe parallel work by themselves. Independent scopes do.
If I ask the terminal agent to refactor authentication while I change authentication in the IDE, I have created a merge meeting with a machine. Even when Git resolves the text, the two changes may encode different assumptions.
I prefer missions with a clean boundary: a test directory, a worker, a documentation surface, a dependency audit, or a bug whose affected path is unlikely to intersect my current edit.
A terminal agent also needs stop conditions. If the root cause points outside the authorized scope, if a required service is unavailable, or if the change demands a product decision, it should stop and report the fork. Silent expansion is not initiative. It is unreviewed authority.
The handoff protocol matters more than either tool
Two agents become useful when they share repository facts without sharing one giant conversation.
I do not try to synchronize their private reasoning. I synchronize the work contract.
The repository should hold durable instructions that both seats can read. This may include project commands, architectural boundaries, testing expectations, generated file rules, and areas that require explicit approval.
Keep those instructions short enough to survive contact with a real task. A forty-page agent manual becomes decorative. The useful version answers questions that recur:
Where may the agent edit?
Which commands prove the change?
Which generated files must not be hand edited?
Which decisions require a human?
What must the completion report contain?
For each mission, I add a temporary ownership declaration.
Mission owner: terminal agent
Scope: packages/webhooks, packages/ledger, related tests
Human active scope: dashboard UI
Shared files: none expected
Stop if: schema or public API change is required
That small block prevents more trouble than a clever prompt library.
The return handoff should be equally mechanical:
Result: completed, blocked, or partial
Cause: one paragraph
Changed: file list with purpose
Verified: exact commands and observed results
Not verified: omitted checks with reason
Review first: risky lines or decisions
Follow up: remaining work
I read the diff before accepting the prose summary. Agent explanations can sound coherent while the patch carries a different story.
My review order is:
Confirm the agent stayed inside scope.
Inspect deletions and public behavior changes.
Read the regression test.
Read the implementation against that test.
Re-run the highest value check when risk warrants it.
Integrate or reject the mission as one unit.
The IDE agent can help during this review, but it does not inherit ownership of the mission. I may ask it to explain a suspicious block or compare the patch with a local contract. I avoid asking it to casually repair the terminal agent’s work before I understand the failure.
Otherwise, the review surface becomes a third implementation path.
Context also needs a direction.
Durable repository rules flow to both seats. Mission facts return through the terminal report and diff. Local design choices made in the IDE should be written into the repository or mission brief before the terminal seat depends on them.
Do not use chat memory as infrastructure.
A clean handoff lets each agent start with less context. That is good. Context should be selected for the task, not accumulated because deletion feels risky.
The second seat pays rent only under specific conditions
I add the terminal seat when it removes a mission, not when it adds another place to type prompts.
The clearest rent-paying case is parallel work with low overlap. I can work on a product decision in the IDE while the terminal agent repairs a separate test failure, audits a dependency change, or prepares a bounded refactor.
Another good case is verification-heavy work.
Tasks that require repeated search, edit, test, and inspect cycles can consume time without needing continuous human judgment. A terminal agent can own that loop, then return the evidence needed for review.
The split also works when interruption is expensive. I may be holding a fragile model of an unfamiliar subsystem. Sending a separate repository task to the terminal keeps command output and investigation branches out of the live IDE thread.
Large repositories create another opening. The IDE seat stays precise near the active code while the terminal seat handles broad discovery:
Trace every use of a deprecated interface
Map which tests cover a worker path
Find configuration drift across packages
Identify the smallest safe dependency upgrade set
Compare an implementation against repository policy
The terminal agent does not need edit permission for every mission. Read-only investigation can pay rent when it returns a sharp map.
I use a simple value estimate:
Rent paid = attention returned + elapsed time saved + avoided rework
Rent burned = subscription cost + review time + collisions + recovery work
This is an estimate, not a benchmark.
The hard variable is attention returned. If I watch the terminal agent, answer five avoidable questions, and repair its patch, elapsed time may look faster while the operator cost gets worse.
I track a few plain signals over several missions:
How many missions reached a reviewable result without scope expansion?
How often did the two seats touch the same files?
How much of the returned diff survived review?
Did verification catch a real issue before handoff?
Did I keep useful focus while the mission ran?
Would manual execution have been easier?
No percentage threshold travels well across teams. A senior engineer in a mature monorepo has different economics from a solo builder exploring a new product. The audit exists to expose your local pattern.
As-of 2026 pattern: model capability is rising faster than many teams are improving task boundaries. That makes seat count a poor proxy for throughput. The builder with one clear protocol can outperform the builder with five agents competing for the same vague task.
Add the second seat after you can describe the work it will own.
Dual stack burns money through collisions, supervision, and weak work
The most common failure is duplicate jurisdiction.
Both agents can edit everything, so both agents eventually do. One changes an interface while the other updates a caller against the old contract. Each patch looks reasonable alone. Integration creates the defect.
The fix is explicit ownership with a shared file check before parallel work begins.
The second failure is mission theater. The task sounds substantial but lacks a finish line:
Improve the architecture and clean up anything related.
An agent can spend a long time producing a large diff that cannot be judged against a concrete outcome. Broad prompts create broad review.
The fix is to name the observed problem, allowed surface, invariants, checks, and stop conditions.
A third failure is permanent supervision. If you keep polling the mission, reading every command, and redirecting minor choices, you have not delegated. You have moved pair programming into a less responsive interface.
The fix may be a better mission brief. It may also be admitting that the task belongs in the IDE because the decisions are too coupled to your live reasoning.
Then comes verification cosplay. The agent says tests passed, but it ran a narrow command that skipped the affected package. Or it added a test that proves its chosen implementation rather than the required behavior.
Ask for exact commands and observed results. Inspect whether the regression test fails for the original reason. Label any check that could not run.
Context duplication burns money more quietly. Both seats receive the full product history, architecture essay, prior transcripts, and unrelated constraints. Prompt cost rises, stale instructions survive, and neither agent knows which facts control the current task.
Give each seat the smallest authoritative context that supports its job.
I would not run two seats for:
A small repository where missions finish before handoff overhead pays back
Early exploration where the architecture changes every few minutes
One tightly coupled feature with no clean file boundary
High risk changes that need continuous domain judgment
Work without reliable checks or review capacity
A team that has not defined basic repository commands
A builder who accepts agent output without reading diffs
I also collapse back to one seat during incidents. When production behavior is changing and evidence arrives minute by minute, one controlled investigation can beat parallel speculation. A second agent may still run a read only search, but it should not create a competing repair path.
The honest limit is that two agents do not solve poor engineering control.
They do not create testability, clarify product intent, repair hidden architecture, or make generated code trustworthy. They increase the rate at which your existing operating quality becomes visible.
If your repository has weak boundaries, the agents will cross them faster.
Use the Two-Agent Seat Map before buying another seat
Copy this checklist into your repository notes, task template, or personal operating file.
Two-Agent Seat Map
Define the IDE seat.
Owns code connected to my current cursor and active reasoning
Handles local explanation, completion, focused refactors, and nearby tests
Expects frequent human steering
Does not start broad repository edits during an active mission
Returns control after each small, inspectable change
Define the terminal seat.
Owns bounded repository missions with a stated finish line
May search, edit, run commands, and verify within named scope
Works without continuous supervision
Stops before expanding scope or making product decisions
Returns a diff plus evidence, not a completion claim alone
Declare ownership before parallel work.
IDE active files:
Terminal mission files:
Shared files expected:
Shared files prohibited:
Human decision owner:
Stop condition:
Write the terminal mission.
Observed problem:
Desired end state:
Allowed scope:
Behavior that must remain unchanged:
Required checks:
Forbidden changes:
Completion report:
Escalation trigger:
Gate the handoff.
Mission status is completed, blocked, or partial
Root cause or rationale is stated
Every changed file has a purpose
Exact verification commands are listed
Failed and skipped checks are visible
Risky decisions are marked for first review
No unrelated cleanup entered the diff
Review in order.
Confirm scope
Inspect deletions and contract changes
Read regression coverage
Read implementation
Re-run the highest value check
Accept, revise, or reject the mission as one unit
Audit whether the seat earns rent.
Did it return meaningful attention?
Did its diff survive review?
Did it avoid collision with active work?
Did verification improve confidence?
Was the mission easier to review than to perform?
Should this task type return to the IDE next time?
You should see two distinct queues: small interactive moves near the cursor and bounded missions with independent verification. If every task could land in either queue, tighten the seat definitions.
Run the audit after several real missions, not after one impressive demo. Keep the second seat when it repeatedly returns focus and reviewable work. Collapse the stack when it creates coordination debt.
Two agents are not a badge of sophistication. They are two different tools for two different shapes of attention.
Use the IDE agent to stay in motion.
Use the terminal agent to send work away with a contract.
Save the Two-Agent Seat Map, run it against your next mission, and let the surviving diff decide whether the second seat stays.
